papers.title: Mediator CKM and MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 reinforce auxin responsiveness to sustain MUTE expression during stomatal lineage differentiation
papers.abstract: Abstract MUTE functions as a pivotal transcription factor that governs the transition from self-renewal to differentiation in meristemoids during stomatal development. This transition requires MUTE expression to reach a critical threshold, yet the mechanisms that maintain its expression homeostasis remain unclear. Here, we show that the Mediator CDK8 kinase module (CKM) acts as a transcriptional coactivator of the MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 complex to regulate meristemoid fate. Specifically, CKM cooperates with MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 to promote the transcription of the auxin-responsive genes, such as SAUR52 and SAUR53, thereby enhancing local auxin response in meristemoids. AUXIN RESPONSE FACTORs (ARFs), including ARF6, ARF7, and ARF19, then bind to MUTE promoter and contribute to its transcription, establishing a positive feedback loop. Disruption of CKM or MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 components reduces SAUR52/53 expression and auxin responses, leading to decreased MUTE transcription, excessive meristemoid self-renewal divisions and arrested differentiation. These defects can be partially rescued by exogenous auxin application or by overexpression of SAUR53 in the mutants. Together, our results uncover a self-reinforcing transcriptional-auxin circuit in which CKM-assisted MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 amplifies auxin response, and auxin reciprocally sustains MUTE expression. This feedback mechanism ensures that MUTE reaches the threshold required to terminate meristemoid self-renewal and initiate differentiation, revealing how transcriptional regulation and hormone signaling are integrated to control stem cell-like behaviors during tissue patterning.

papers.title: Photosynthesis-derived carbon gates cell cycle activation to enable hormone-autonomous shoot regeneration
papers.abstract: Abstract Shoot regeneration is a powerful model for cell fate reprogramming but how it occurs in nature remains poorly understood because studies in Arabidopsis thaliana conventionally rely on in vitro assays supplemented with exogenous hormones and sugars. Here, we established the Hormone-autonomY Direct Regeneration Assay (HYDRA) in which removal of the shoot apical meristem (SAM) initiates shoot regeneration from the cotyledon-hypocotyl boundary without hormone or sugar supplementation. We identify photosynthesis-derived carbon and the boundary domain as two separable but convergent requirements for shoot regeneration in HYDRA. Following SAM removal, carbon availability increases in the boundary domain where it activates cell-cycle progression via the RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED1 (RBR1) pathway. Carbon deprivation blocks regeneration despite induction of shoot meristem genes, indicating proliferative activation is limiting. Pre-existing shoot-competent boundary cells give rise to regenerated shoots upon cell-cycle activation, while their perturbation impairs regeneration despite sufficient carbon. Carbon therefore gates the proliferative activation of these cells, enabling functional shoot meristem formation. Additionally, exogenous carbon supply overcomes the requirement for SAM removal to induce shoot formation, indicating that carbon availability also acts as an initiation cue. Together, this study reveals an inherent capacity for hormone-autonomous shoot regeneration and identifies photosynthesis-derived carbon as a central regulator of this process.

papers.title: Natural product biosynthesis by guanidine prenyltransferases in plants and bacteria
papers.abstract: Guanidine exists almost exclusively as a resonance-stabilized cation, making its direct enzymatic functionalization challenging. We identified the cyanobacterial enzyme NosH, which catalyzes direct prenyl transfer to free guanidine. Structural and mechanistic analyses revealed guanidine activation by a two-aspartate clamp coupled to prenyl-donor binding through a distinct catalytic architecture. Guided by these features, we identified a large family of guanidine prenyltransferases across bacteria and plants. Plant enzymes produced guanidine alkaloids such as galegine in vitro and heterologous expression of a plant ortholog in Nicotiana benthamiana produced galegine in planta, providing a direct enzymatic link to plant-specialized metabolism.

papers.title: Near-complete assembly of wild emmer wheat unveils centromere reorganization during polyploid evolution
Reduction of aflatoxin contamination in maize kernels mediated by host-induced gene silencing
papers.abstract: Aflatoxins produced by some species of Aspergillus pose a significant threat to global food safety, because they contaminate a variety of crops including maize. In this study, we used host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) to reduce aflatoxin accumulation in maize upon infection with Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus . Two RNAi constructs were designed and introduced into maize, one targeting two essential fungal genes involved in ergosterol biosynthesis ( CYP51A and CYP51B ) and the other targeting three aflatoxin biosynthesis genes ( AflC , AflD , and AflR ). The presence of RNAi transgenes was confirmed in 17 and 14 independent lines possessing the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi construct and the AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi construct, respectively. Most transgenic lines had single-locus integrations and one or two copies of the transgene. Transgene expression varied considerably among the lines. Small RNA sequencing confirmed the production of siRNAs from the HIGS trigger sequences. Levels of CYP51A , AflC , AflD, and AflR transcripts in Aspergillus spp. were successfully decreased upon infection of transgenic maize. However, significant reduction in the level of CYP51B transcripts was not achieved and the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi transgene had no discernible effect on fungal growth in infected maize. In contrast, we observed significant reductions in aflatoxin accumulation in four AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi transgenic lines infected with A. flavus and in two transgenic lines infected with A. parasiticus . Notably, one AflC/AflD/AflR transgenic line exhibited minimal aflatoxin contamination upon kernel infection with A. parasiticus . These results demonstrate the potential of HIGS to reduce aflatoxin production in mature corn kernels.

papers.title: Can plants defend coasts against storms?
Evolution of the arbuscular mycorrhizal regulatory network through differential GRAS gene retention and protein interaction in land plants
papers.abstract: Plants rely on an ancient genetic “toolkit” to establish arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis (AMS) with fungal partners. However, the symbiotic outcomes vary among AMS hosts, indicating divergence in downstream transcriptional reprogramming after the perception of symbiotic signals. To uncover the cross-species variation of the AMS regulatory network, we traced the evolutionary trajectory of the GRAS gene family, which encodes the major group of transcription factors in AMS regulation. Phylogenetic analysis of the GRAS family across land plants placed known symbiotic GRAS members within 12 anciently diverged lineages, with multiple lineages showing pronounced gene loss in nonmycorrhizal plants. This pattern pointed to three additional GRAS lineages as candidates for AMS regulation. Given that tomato harbors single-copy, AMS-induced genes in these lineages, we selected it for functional validation. CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis, combined with detailed phenotyping of fungal colonization and arbuscule morphology, and transcriptome profiling of mutant roots, confirmed that all three tomato genes are individually required for AMS development, designated Symbiosis-Required GRAS (SRG) 1 to 3. Large-scale phylogenomic analysis and protein interaction assays (by yeast two-hybrid and bimolecular fluorescence complementation) further showed that both the repertoire and interaction networks of symbiotic GRAS members vary among AMS hosts. In summary, together with 12 previously characterized lineages, the three SRGs identified in this study bring the total number of GRAS lineages with known symbiotic members across land plants to fifteen. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the symbiotic GRAS network has been dynamically reshaped by gene loss and rewiring of protein interactions during land plant evolution.
